q: A sharp, well-maintained classroom sends so many wonderful and powerful messages to students—from an expectation of excellence to personal pride in their work habits.

For students take their cue from you, the leader of the classroom. And just as a tidy, clutter-free environment conveys a message of respect and politeness and attention to detail, a messy room signals to all who enter that mediocrity is okay.
So what is this thought, this key to organization? It is efficiency.
The truth is, you need far less ‘stuff’ than you think you do. Good teaching has little to do with the accumulation of materials.
But the real power of organizing your classroom with efficiency as your guide is the impact it will have on your students.

t: 5 Classroom Management Tips For Every Teacher
q: Well-taught routines, performed with excellence, are among the clearest indicators of exceptional teaching.
An inconsistently followed classroom management plan is one of the most common teacher mistakes. It’s also among the most detrimental.
If you're merely pleasant in your interactions with students, if you're open to laughter and seeing the humor in your classroom... then behavior-influencing rapport will grow naturally.
Most teachers talk too much, help too much, and are seen too much. The truth is, micromanagement breeds needy, demanding, and dependent students.
But in the end, blaming parents, video games, or the neighborhood they live in, for example, solves nothing and makes creating the classroom you really want an impossibility.
It’s scary to step out into the unknown. It’s scary to dare yourself to be more than just another teacher.

t: How To Handle Students Who Tattle, Complain, And Need Your Frequent Attention n-and-need-your-frequent-attention/
q: The student is one of several who frequently need your attention—to tell on a classmate, voice a complaint, or ask why he gets to do this or she gets to do that.
But in the long run, an exasperated response will only cause their complaining and tattling to worsen.
Effective teaching requires you to never let the whole of your class suffer because of a small few.
By showing that you care, by validating their concerns and perturbations, your students will be free to let them go, focus on their academic responsibilities.
It may seem counterintuitive, but the best way to curb the intensity and frequency of tattling is to take it seriously.
But when they know they can count on you to safeguard their right to learn and enjoy school without interference, they’ll lay down their sword.

t: Why It’s Okay To Let Your Students Experience Failure e-failure/
q: The truth is, our students are far better off when allowed to experience their mistakes, failures, and defeats.
We do our students a disservice by interfering with the normal, human, and energy-producing powers of regret.
We owe it to our students not to minimize failure, but to allow them to feel it.
A meaningless ‘C’ when they deserve an ‘F’ is not only dishonest, but it’s harmful.
Now is the time, when the stakes are low, to build the fortitude needed to overcome that closed door, that letter of rejection, that loss of job.
They need to experience failure now, in the safety of your loving guidance, so that it doesn’t crush them in the future.
